strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in conditional diffusion sampling: improving prompt alignment and global coherence at inference time without retraining the generator.

The proposed Ctrl-Z Sampling is simple and model-agnostic in spirit, combining reward-triggered exploration, random latent inversion, candidate evaluation, and adaptive rollback depth. This is a reasonable extension of resampling, zigzag sampling, and reward-guided search methods.

The manuscript includes comparisons against DDIM, Resampling, Z-Sampling, and SOP on Pick-a-Pic and DrawBench, plus ablations over reward models, exploration triggers, rollback depth, and acceptance thresholds.

Results are directionally consistent: Ctrl-Z improves all reported automatic metrics over DDIM and prior sampling baselines, and is reported to be more NFE-efficient than SOP while achieving higher ImageReward and modestly better HPS/PickScore/AES.
The paper is generally readable, and Algorithm 1 gives a useful high-level description of the sampling procedure.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. Under that bar, the novelty appears incremental: the core idea is an adaptive-depth reward-guided search over noisy latent rollbacks, closely related to SOP, zigzag/resampling, and recent inference-time scaling methods. The paper does not sharply distinguish the algorithmic contribution from simply spending reward-model-guided compute at different depths.

The evidence relies entirely on automatic preference/reward metrics, and the largest gains are on ImageReward, which is also used to guide the search. This creates a reward-hacking/evaluation leakage concern. There is no human preference study or independent evaluation strong enough to validate the claimed improvements in alignment and visual quality.

The experimental scope is narrow: only Stable Diffusion 2.1, two prompt sets, and 500/200 prompts are used. The claim of broad applicability to diffusion frameworks is not demonstrated on stronger modern text-to-image models, different samplers/solvers, image editing, video, or other conditional generation settings.

The compute tradeoff is underdeveloped. A 7.6x increase in NFEs is called moderate, but wall-clock latency, GPU memory, batching behavior, and quality-vs-compute curves are not reported in enough detail. Comparisons to SOP and other test-time scaling baselines are not fully normalized across compute budgets.

Several method details are unclear or potentially inconsistent. The algorithm states unbounded search depth by default, yet termination is not rigorously guaranteed when dmax is infinity; the text says the candidate budget per inversion step guarantees termination, which is not true for an unbounded number of depths. There are also notation ambiguities around evaluating the candidate clean estimate after inversion/redenosing.

The interpretation of diffusion sampling as hill climbing and local maxima escape is mostly heuristic. The paper does not provide theoretical analysis or empirical diagnostics showing that the detected reward plateaus correspond to meaningful local optima rather than noise in reward estimates.

Ablations are useful but incomplete. Important missing studies include sensitivity to exploration window lambda, number of candidates N/Nb under fixed compute, reward threshold calibration, random seed variance, statistical significance, and failure cases where reward-guided rollback harms image fidelity or diversity.

Reproducibility is only partial: the paper lists major hyperparameters and hardware, but does not provide enough implementation detail for batching, exact schedules, stopping behavior, random seeds, or released code/data splits. The qualitative evidence is also quite limited.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple inference-time sampling idea for diffusion models: detect reward stagnation, roll the latent state back to noisier timesteps with random perturbations, and greedily accept candidates with improved reward. The high-level mechanism is intuitive and plausibly useful as a model-agnostic wrapper around DDIM-style sampling.

The manuscript includes comparisons against relevant nearby sampling/search baselines, including DDIM, resampling, Z-Sampling, and SOP, and reports both prompt-alignment and aesthetic metrics on Pick-a-Pic and DrawBench.

The ablations over reward model choice, exploration trigger, threshold, and inversion depth are useful and show that the method’s behavior is at least partially characterized. The qualitative examples also illustrate the intended failure mode of escaping semantically misaligned generations.
weaknesses: The novelty over recent reward-guided test-time search methods appears limited. The method is essentially an adaptive-depth stochastic rollback/search procedure, and the paper does not make a strong case that the conceptual advance over SOP, Z-Sampling, restart/resampling, or broader inference-time scaling work is substantial enough for ECCV.

The experimental evidence is not convincing enough for the claims. The main evaluation is almost entirely based on automatic reward/preference models, while ImageReward is also used to guide the search. This creates a serious risk of reward-model overfitting or metric gaming. There is no human preference study, no blind pairwise evaluation, and no analysis of cases where reward improvement hurts perceived quality.

The gains over the strongest baseline are small on most non-optimized metrics. For example, on Pick-a-Pic the improvement over SOP is 0.2671 to 0.2678 HPSv2, 5.687 to 5.697 AES, and 20.896 to 20.913 PickScore. The largest margins are on ImageReward, the guiding reward, so the reported improvements do not clearly establish perceptual or semantic superiority.

The computational cost remains high. A 7.6x NFE increase is described as moderate, but this is a major latency cost for practical text-to-image inference. The paper does not report wall-clock time, memory, batching behavior, variance across prompts, or quality-vs-compute curves sufficient to judge whether the method is actually preferable to simply sampling more seeds or using other test-time scaling strategies.

The comparison protocol is under-specified and potentially unfair. SOP is set to 5 candidates to match NFEs approximately, but Ctrl-Z has adaptive unrestricted depth and up to 20 candidates per step; the exact NFE distributions, stopping behavior, and equal-compute comparisons are not fully reported. Standard deviations, confidence intervals, and significance tests are absent despite small metric differences.

The method is evaluated narrowly: only Stable Diffusion 2.1, two prompt sets, and DDIM-style sampling are considered. The paper claims broad applicability, but does not test stronger modern generators, alternative solvers, other guidance scales, higher resolutions, negative prompts, or non-text-to-image settings.

The algorithmic description has indexing and clarity issues. The pseudocode mixes states xt, xt-1, and candidate estimates in ways that are difficult to reproduce, and the “unbounded” dmax claim is questionable without a precise termination bound beyond practical schedule limits. Important implementation details such as reward evaluation on decoded intermediate x0 estimates, VAE decoding cost, random seeds, and candidate batching are not sufficiently specified.

The hill-climbing/local-maxima framing is mostly metaphorical. The paper does not provide theoretical analysis or empirical diagnostics showing that diffusion trajectories actually encounter local maxima in a reward landscape, nor that the proposed criterion reliably detects them rather than merely responding to noisy reward fluctuations.

The qualitative evidence is sparse and hand-picked. Figure 3 contains only a few examples and does not show failure cases, diversity changes, artifacts introduced by rollback, or whether improvements are consistent across random seeds.

The paper lacks discussion of limitations and societal impact. For a reward-guided generative sampling method, the risk of amplifying reward-model biases, preference-model artifacts, and prompt-dependent failure modes should be addressed.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and practically useful inference-time sampling strategy for conditional diffusion models. Ctrl-Z Sampling is model-agnostic, training-free, and conceptually easy to integrate: detect reward stagnation, inject controlled noise by rolling back to a noisier latent state, and accept reward-improving continuations.

The method is well motivated relative to resampling, Z-Sampling, and search-over-path approaches. The adaptive rollback depth is a sensible contribution because it targets cases where shallow perturbations are insufficient, while avoiding exhaustive search at every step.

Empirical results are consistently positive on Pick-a-Pic and DrawBench across HPS v2, AES, PickScore, and ImageReward. The gains over DDIM and related baselines are modest but steady, and the comparison to SOP is particularly relevant because both use reward-guided inference-time search.

The ablations are useful: the paper studies reward model choice, exploration trigger policy, maximum inversion depth, and acceptance threshold. These experiments support the claim that the approach is not tied to a single reward model and that reward-based triggering provides a quality/compute tradeoff.

The paper is generally readable, with an explicit algorithm and intuitive figures. The contribution type is best treated as Algorithms/General, and the evidence is appropriate for a sampling-method paper rather than a new model-training paper.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is still somewhat narrow. All main experiments use Stable Diffusion 2.1 with only two prompt benchmarks, and there is no evidence on stronger modern generators, different schedulers, higher-resolution settings, image-editing/control tasks, or non-text-to-image diffusion domains despite broad claims of generality.

Evaluation relies entirely on automatic preference/reward metrics, and ImageReward is both the main exploration reward and one of the primary reported metrics. Although the paper also reports HPS v2, PickScore, and AES, a human preference study or held-out reward evaluation would make the improvement less vulnerable to reward overfitting or metric gaming concerns.

The computational overhead remains substantial: 7.6x NFEs is described as moderate, but this may be impractical for many local inference settings. The paper reports NFEs but not wall-clock latency, memory/batching details, variance, or worst-case behavior, and the Always baseline suggests substantially better quality is available at much higher cost.

The novelty is incremental relative to recent inference-time search, resampling, restart, and zigzag methods. The adaptive depth mechanism is useful, but the paper would benefit from a sharper distinction from SOP and other 2025 test-time scaling/search methods beyond qualitative intuition and one fixed-NFE comparison.

Some technical details need tightening. The algorithm has potential indexing ambiguities around the candidate clean estimate and accepted state, and the statement that an unbounded default search depth still guarantees termination is not fully convincing unless the maximum reachable timestep or a global budget is specified. The hill-climbing/local-maxima interpretation is intuitive but not theoretically substantiated.

The paper does not discuss failure cases, sensitivity to reward miscalibration, possible degradation of diversity, or societal risks from using preference models to steer generation. These omissions do not invalidate the method, but they leave important deployment behavior underexplored.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and practical inference-time sampling method for text-to-image diffusion models. Ctrl-Z Sampling adaptively detects reward stagnation, rolls back to noisier latent states, and searches progressively deeper when shallow perturbations fail, which is a sensible extension of resampling, zigzag, and search-over-path ideas.

The method is model-agnostic and demonstrated on both a U-Net-based model, Stable Diffusion 2.1, and a Transformer-based model, Hunyuan-DiT. This cross-architecture evaluation strengthens the claim that the approach is not tied to one sampler implementation.

The empirical results are reasonably broad, covering Pick-a-Pic, DrawBench, and T2I-CompBench, with several automatic preference/alignment metrics. Ctrl-Z generally improves over DDIM, Resampling, Z-Sampling, and SOP, especially on compositional categories in T2I-CompBench.

The ablation study is useful: the paper investigates exploration depth, number of candidates, reward model choice, exploration initiation criteria, acceptance threshold, and exploration window. These experiments support the core design choice that adaptive depth can be more efficient than purely wider candidate search.

The paper is mostly clear and includes implementation details such as sampling steps, guidance scale, exploration window, maximum candidates, maximum depth, reward model, software versions, and hardware, which helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The contribution is mainly a reward-guided adaptive rollback/deeper search heuristic built from existing ingredients: DDIM inversion/noise reinjection, reward-guided test-time search, resampling, and zigzag sampling. The paper’s hill-climbing/local-maxima framing is intuitive, but not rigorously validated.

The improvements over the strongest baseline SOP are often small on the main preference metrics. For example, on Stable Diffusion 2.1, Ctrl-Z is only marginally better than SOP on HPSv2 and ImageReward and slightly worse on PickScore; on Hunyuan-DiT, SOP is competitive or better on some metrics. The case for acceptance depends on the efficiency and CompBench gains rather than a large quality jump.

The evaluation is heavily based on learned reward/preference metrics, and ImageReward is also used to guide the method. This creates a risk of reward-model overfitting or metric circularity. The paper would be much stronger with human preference studies or evaluation by stronger independent vision-language judges not used for optimization.

The reported computational overhead remains high for practical deployment: around 7-9x NFEs in the main setting. The paper reports NFEs but does not provide wall-clock latency, memory overhead, batching behavior, or a quality-vs-time comparison, which are important for an inference-time scaling method.

Several experimental choices limit the strength of the evidence. The method is not tested on stronger contemporary text-to-image systems such as SDXL-class or newer diffusion/flow models, and comparisons to orthogonal fast samplers or combined solver settings are left out. Baseline tuning under equal wall-clock or equal reward-query budgets is also not fully established.

The algorithm and exposition contain some ambiguities and minor inconsistencies. The local maximum criterion is described as falling below the previous best, but implemented as requiring non-decreasing reward; the pseudocode acceptance condition appears to check the last candidate rather than the best candidate; and details such as exact timestep indexing, rollback state choice, and stochastic inversion behavior could be specified more carefully.

The paper discusses limitations, but important failure modes remain underexplored: reward hacking, degraded diversity, sensitivity to prompt type, cases where deeper rollback destroys useful structure, and whether repeated reward selection biases outputs toward aesthetic or preference-model artifacts.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in diffusion inference: improving prompt alignment and global consistency at test time without retraining the generator.

The proposed Ctrl-Z sampler is simple and broadly applicable in principle: it combines reward-guided candidate selection with adaptive rollback/noise injection, and is demonstrated on both SD 2.1 and Hunyuan-DiT.
The manuscript includes several useful ablations over reward models, exploration depth/width, exploration windows, and initiation criteria, which help characterize the method’s behavior.
The results show some consistent gains over DDIM, resampling, Z-Sampling, and SOP on automated preference/compositional metrics, especially ImageReward and T2I-CompBench categories.
weaknesses: The central conceptual framing is weakly supported. Diffusion denoising is repeatedly described as hill climbing in a reward landscape and failures as local maxima, but this is largely metaphorical; the paper does not provide a rigorous analysis or convincing empirical evidence that the proposed mechanism actually detects or escapes such optima.

Originality is limited. The method appears to be an incremental combination of prior rollback/resampling, zigzag/restart sampling, and reward-guided test-time search. The distinction from SOP and related inference-time scaling methods is mostly adaptive depth versus fixed candidate search, which is useful but not enough to make a strong contribution as presented.

The evaluation is heavily dependent on learned reward/proxy metrics, and the main method often optimizes or selects using ImageReward while also reporting ImageReward as a headline metric. This creates a serious risk of reward overfitting and makes the largest reported gains less persuasive. There is no human evaluation to validate that the reward improvements correspond to genuine perceptual or semantic improvements.

Reported improvements on non-optimized metrics are often small or mixed. For example, Ctrl-Z is not consistently best on PickScore, AES, or some Hunyuan-DiT/T2I-CompBench categories, while requiring roughly 7-9x more denoising evaluations plus reward-model evaluations. The paper does not report wall-clock cost, memory overhead, or parallelization assumptions, so the practicality claim is under-supported.

The comparison to baselines is not fully convincing. SOP is given one fixed candidate setting and is sometimes cited inconsistently; stronger budget-matched variants, modern solvers, and broader test-time scaling baselines are missing. Since Ctrl-Z adds an extra depth dimension, it should be compared against equally tuned width/depth/budget alternatives rather than a narrow SOP configuration.

The algorithm and text contain inconsistencies that affect technical clarity. The paper says the default inversion depth is unbounded, but experiments use dmax=3; the algorithm appears to test the last candidate score rather than the best candidate at the break condition; and after failed exploration it updates rprev to the best found score even if it does not satisfy the claimed non-decreasing acceptance rule.

Experimental reporting is incomplete for reproducibility and reliability. The paper lacks variance/error bars, seed counts, statistical tests, exact prompt sampling details, wall-clock timings, and sufficient implementation details for baseline parity. Qualitative examples are few and likely cherry-picked.

The writing and presentation have numerous grammar, notation, and formatting problems, including malformed equations/text, inconsistent names, and unclear definitions. These issues do not by themselves determine rejection, but they compound the difficulty of assessing the scientific claim.

The limitations section acknowledges scheduling and scaling issues, but the core weaknesses remain unresolved: the method may simply spend substantially more compute to optimize imperfect reward models, with unclear generalization to real human preference or production-relevant inference budgets.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and practically relevant inference-time sampling method for conditional diffusion generation: reward-guided adaptive backward exploration with increasing inversion depth when local search fails. The method is model-agnostic and conceptually simple enough to be integrated into existing DDIM-style pipelines.

The empirical evidence is reasonably strong. Results are reported on Pick-a-Pic, DrawBench, and T2I-CompBench, using both Stable Diffusion 2.1 and Hunyuan-DiT, and the method generally improves human-aligned metrics, compositional scores, and qualitative prompt alignment over DDIM, resampling, Z-Sampling, and SOP.

The ablation study is a notable strength. The paper analyzes exploration depth, candidate width, reward-model choice, initiation criteria, exploration window, acceptance threshold, and cross-architecture behavior. These experiments support the main claim that deeper adaptive exploration can be more efficient than simply widening shallow candidate search.

The paper is mostly well organized and includes useful implementation details in the supplementary material, including datasets, metrics, hyperparameters, baselines, software versions, and hardware. The limitations section is also meaningful, especially around fixed reward thresholds and incomplete inference-scaling validation.

The qualitative examples are consistent with the quantitative story: Ctrl-Z appears especially helpful for spatial relations, counting, color/attribute binding, and globally coherent prompt following.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than decisive. The method is a thoughtful combination of existing ideas: resampling, zigzag/restart-style inversion, reward-guided search, and test-time scaling. The adaptive increase in inversion depth is useful, but the paper could more sharply distinguish its technical contribution from SOP and related inference-time search methods.

The hill-climbing/local-maxima interpretation is intuitive but informal. The paper relies on this framing to motivate the method, yet provides no theoretical characterization of the reward landscape, no evidence that detected plateaus correspond to true local maxima, and no analysis of when backward noising preserves useful structure versus disrupting it.

The evaluation depends heavily on automatic reward/preference metrics, and ImageReward is also used as the main guidance signal. Although the paper reports gains on other metrics, the strongest improvements are often on the optimized reward itself. A human preference study, or at least stronger safeguards against reward-model overoptimization, would make the empirical case more convincing.

The computational cost remains substantial: roughly 7-9x NFEs in the main setting, and higher for always-explore variants. The paper frames this as moderate and more efficient than SOP, but does not provide enough wall-clock latency, memory, batching, or parallelization analysis to establish practicality for local inference.

Some algorithmic details are potentially confusing or underspecified. For example, the acceptance rule is described as enforcing non-decreasing reward when delta=0, but the algorithm appears to update to the best candidate found even if it does not exceed the previous accepted reward, which may allow reward decreases. The treatment of unbounded versus fixed dmax is also inconsistent between the method text and experiments.

Experimental coverage is good but not complete. The paper does not compare with some orthogonal modern samplers or combined settings, does not report statistical uncertainty, and only lightly explores larger inference-scaling regimes despite positioning the method as a test-time scaling strategy. Code availability is also not discussed in the manuscript.
